Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)

Reflux of gastric contents into the lower esophagus because the barrier at the gastroesophageal junction fails.

Slide 4GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE
  • GERD is often associated with a hiatal hernia
  • the most common is the type I hernia, also called a sliding hiatal hernia
  • Type II and III hiatal hernias are often referred to as para-esophageal hernias and they may be associated with GERD
  • Type IV when there is other organ herniated into the chest (Spleen ,Colon)

Notes

Hiatus hernia types

TypeNameGE junctionWhat herniates
Type ISlidingAbove the diaphragmGE junction itself slides up
Type IITrue paraesophagealBelow the diaphragm (stays in place)Stomach, usually the fundus, herniates alongside the esophagus
Type IIIMixed (I + II)Above the diaphragmGE junction and part of the stomach
Type IVComplexVariableAnother abdominal organ besides stomach — omentum, colon, pancreas, spleen
TERMINOLOGY
A paraesophageal hernia is one type of hiatus hernia, not a synonym for all of them. In a type II hernia with a still-competent LES, the patient may have epigastric pain and vomiting without any reflux.
  • Type IV hiatus hernia → a structure other than stomach (omentum, colon, small bowel). 438

Notes

Definition & pathophysiology

CORE MECHANISM
GERD = reflux of gastric contents into the lower esophagus due to an incompetent LES ± hiatus hernia.
Content moves from the high-pressure abdomen to the low / negative-pressure chest — a suction effect once the LES barrier is incompetent.
The refluxate is not only acid: acid, alkaline contents, bile, pepsin, enzymes and food.
A chronic, relapsing disease causing mucosal injury and potential complications.
RULE OF THUMB
Hiatus hernia and GERD are not the same thing. GERD can occur without a hiatus hernia, and a hiatus hernia commonly — but not invariably — causes GERD.

Clinical presentation

Typical symptoms

Heartburn and regurgitation.
Worse after food or drink followed by lying supine or changing position.
Often relieved promptly by antacids.

Atypical / extra-esophageal

Aspiration.
Pneumonia.
Laryngitis / ENT manifestations.

These usually indicate more severe, more proximal reflux.

SymptomWhat it should make you think of
DysphagiaPeptic stricture or esophageal cancer

CLASSIC EXAM TRAP: PEPTIC STRICTURE VS PEPTIC ULCER
Peptic stricture = an esophageal disease caused by reflux.
Peptic ulcer = a gastric / duodenal disease, not caused by reflux, commonly associated with H. pylori.
They may coexist in one patient, but one does not cause the other.
  • Overweight 45-year-old with chest discomfort and heartburn, worse with smoking and stress, normal exam → GERD. 436
Exam trap: peptic STRICTURE is caused by reflux (oesophageal); peptic ULCER is gastric/duodenal, not caused by reflux (H. pylori). They can coexist; one doesn't cause the other.
  • Pneumomediastinum with a contained oesophageal leak, stable → NPO + IV antibiotics (conservative). 441
  • Retching after heavy drinking → haematemesis, no liver disease → Mallory–Weiss tear. 442 ×5

Achalasia

Slide 20
  • Achalasia is an uncommon disease of esophageal motility disorder
  • It is characterized by degeneration of the myenteric neurons that innervate LES and esophageal body
  • Possible pathogenesis: hereditary, degenerative, autoimmune, or infectious
  • Incidence: 0.5 per 100,000
  • Prevalence: 1 per 10,000
  • Commonly occurs in: ages 20-50 years. Equal gender distribution

Equal gender distribution

Notes

Pathophysiology

Degeneration of inhibitory myenteric neurons to the LES→Loss of inhibition → persistently contracted LES→Muscular hypertrophy + fibrosis→Obstruction & dysphagia

Possible etiologies

Hereditary
Degenerative
Autoimmune
Infectious — including Chagas disease

Demographics

Classically younger than the typical GERD / hiatus hernia patient.
Symptoms often begin in the 20s to early 30s.
Equal sex distribution.

Clinical features

Slide 21
  • Dysphagia to solids and liquids is the most common presenting symptom, experienced by greater than 90% of patients.
  • regurgitation of food or saliva: second most common symptom, occurring in approximately 60% of patients.
  • chest pain
  • weight loss: end stage disease
  • Heartburn: direct irritation of the Esophageal lining by retained food, pills, or acidic by products of bacterial metabolism of retained food.
  • pulmonary symptoms: Nocturnal regurgitation of esophageal contents can lead to nighttime cough and aspiration.
  • adaptive mechanisms

  • 60-year-old smoker/drinker, dysphagia solids → then liquids, weight loss → oesophageal cancer. 442
Notes

Clinical features

HIGHEST-YIELD DISCRIMINATOR
The most common symptom is dysphagia to BOTH solids and liquids.
Functional / motility dysphagia → solids and liquids from the start.
Mechanical obstruction (tumor, stricture) → initially mainly solids.
Regurgitation — from stagnant food in the esophagus, not from gastric reflux.
Chest pain; heartburn may also occur.
Weight loss in advanced disease.
Pulmonary symptoms and aspiration from retained esophageal contents.
CLINICAL TRAP
Achalasia can present with heartburn and regurgitation and be mislabelled as GERD. Progressive dysphagia may be subtle because patients develop adaptive swallowing habits. The professor specifically discouraged handing out 6 weeks of PPI without establishing the diagnosis in a patient with persistent daily symptoms.
Dysphagia to solids AND liquids = motility (achalasia); solids first → then liquids = mechanical obstruction (cancer, stricture).
  • Dysphagia of achalasia → to solids and liquids. 439

Diagnosis

Slide 22
  • CXR may show air-fluid level
  • Barium study quite dilated, and an air-fluid level may be secondary to retained secretions. The classic finding is a gradual smooth tapering at the end of the Esophagus, similar to a bird's beak.
  • Upper endoscopy: Normal in 50% of achalasia patients
  • Primary role: rule out pseudoachalasia (2ry to malignancy)
  • Findings: Dilated body with retained food and liquids
  • Retention esophagitis with cobble stone mucosa
  • LES tonically closed but possible to pass the scope

CXR may show air-fluid level Barium study quite dilated, and an air-fluid level may be Upper endoscopy: Normal in 50% of achalasia patients Primary role: rule out pseudoachalasia (2ry to malignancy)

Findings: Dilated body with retained food and liquids Retention esophagitis with cobble stone mucosa LES tonically closed but possible to pass the scope

Notes

Investigations

TestFindings and role
Manometry ★Gold standard / test of choice. Achalasia is fundamentally a muscle-function disorder, so the function test makes the diagnosis
Chest X-rayWidened mediastinum from the dilated esophagus; air–fluid level from retained contents
Barium swallowDilated distal esophagus with smooth narrowing at the GE junction — the bird's- beak / rat-tail appearance. Smooth narrowing favors benign disease; malignancy tends to give mucosal irregularity. Characteristic but not the gold standard
Upper endoscopyMainly to exclude pseudo-achalasia, especially malignancy. In true achalasia the scope meets initial resistance at the LES then passes with a characteristic "pop"; cancer gives more persistent, irregular obstruction
WHY ENDOSCOPY STILL MATTERS IN ACHALASIA
Achalasia patients carry an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma, and a reflux-associated adenocarcinoma can also mimic achalasia.
Manometry = gold standard (the doctor: a muscle-function disease is diagnosed by a function test). Barium shows the bird's beak but doesn't make the diagnosis.

Notes

Manometric findings

THE THREE CORE FINDINGS
Hypertensive LES.
Incomplete or absent LES relaxation.
Absent normal peristalsis of the distal esophageal body.
PERISTALSIS IS NOT THE SAME AS CONTRACTION
Peristalsis = coordinated, propagated contractions directed toward the stomach.
Contractions may be present but haphazard and non-propagated — this is why type III achalasia has contractions yet still no normal peristalsis.
Do not write "no contractions" when the answer is "no peristalsis."
TypeManometric picture (types themselves are not required — used only to explain manometry)
Type ITight LES + lax, non-pressurized esophageal body
Type IITight LES + pressurization of the esophageal body
Type IIISpastic, aggressive abnormal contractions
  • 30-year-old, intermittent dysphagia for 5 years, dilated oesophagus with a tight LES → manometry shows high LES pressure. 437 ×6

Treatment

Slide 27
  • The primary therapeutic goal in achalasia is to reduce the LES basal pressure
  • Treatment options include medical therapy, botulinum toxin injection, pneumatic dilation, and surgical or endoscopic myotomy
  • Symptom relief, particularly relief of dysphagia, is accepted as the primary desired outcome

The primary therapeutic goal in achalasia is to reduce the LES Treatment options include medical therapy, botulinum toxin Symptom relief, particularly relief of dysphagia, is accepted as

Notes

Treatment

GOVERNING PRINCIPLE
Achalasia cannot be cured — lost neurons cannot be restored. All treatment is palliative, aimed at decreasing LES pressure.
OptionMechanismLimitation / concern
Nitrates & calcium- channel blockersReduce smooth-muscle contractionLimited LES benefit plus systemic vascular effects — mainly for patients who are poor candidates for definitive intervention
Botulinum toxinInjected into the LES → muscle paralysis/relaxationTemporary — repeat injection every 3–4 months. Achalasia hits young patients, so more durable options are usually preferred
Pneumatic dilatationStrong balloon across the LES tears fibrotic muscle fibers; mucosa and submucosa stretch while the less elastic muscle rupturesGood initial response and equivalent to surgical myotomy for the first 2 years in the RCT discussed; particularly effective in older women. Long term, torn fibers may reconnect, and reflux can follow LES disruption
POEMPeroral endoscopic myotomy: mucosal incision → submucosal tunnel → knife divides the LES/esophageal muscle → mucosa closed. More controlled than dilationGood symptom results, but the major concern is post-procedure GERD — symptomatic reflux in about 40%. PPI suppresses acid but does not prevent reflux of non- acid gastric contents
Surgical myotomy ★Muscle divided longitudinally along the distal esophagus while preserving mucosa and submucosa, followed by a partial fundoplicationThe professor's gold standard.
FUNDOPLICATION AFTER MYOTOMY
The wrap must be partial or omitted — a complete wrap is avoided because the abnormal esophageal motility could create outflow obstruction.
Options: Dor (anterior partial) or Toupet (posterior partial).
The professor prefers Dor: it is the weaker, less obstructive wrap, and it covers the myotomy site, protecting against the consequences of an occult mucosal injury.
NEW DYSPHAGIA YEARS AFTER A SUCCESSFUL MYOTOMY
Cancer risk persists even after successful myotomy. A complete work-up must consider:
Recurrent achalasia.
Reconnection / healing of the divided muscle fibers.
Adenocarcinoma related to post-treatment reflux.
Squamous cell carcinoma related to longstanding achalasia.

Slide 35Surgical Therapy
  • Esophageomyotomy:
  • Goal: reduce LES pressure enough to allow gravity drainage of the esophagus and maintain control of reflux
  • Can be done open or MIS, VATS or Laparoscopy
  • Laparoscopy: shorter length of surgery, shorter length of stay, better dysphagia relief, less post op heartburn, and less incisional discomfort.

  • Uncommon but important secondary complications of achalasia include the formation of epiphrenic diverticula and esophageal cancer.

Esophageal Diverticula

Classified two ways at once: by wall composition (true vs false) and by mechanism (traction vs pulsion).

By wall composition

True diverticulum — contains all esophageal wall layers.
False diverticulum — mucosa/submucosa herniate through a muscular defect.

By mechanism

Traction — pulled from outside.
Pulsion — pushed from inside by pressure.
MNEMONIC: TNT
True = Traction (so False = Pulsion).
True traction: an adjacent inflammatory structure or lymph node adheres to the esophagus; healing and retraction pull the entire wall outward.
False pulsion: increased intraluminal pressure forces mucosa and submucosa through an anatomical muscular weakness.
LocationNameTypeDriving mechanism
UpperZenker diverticulumFalse — pulsionHypertonic cricopharyngeus / upper esophageal sphincter
MiddleTraction diverticulumTrue — tractionAdjacent inflammation / lymph node pulling outward
LowerEpiphrenic diverticulumFalse — pulsionAchalasia / hypertensive LES raising distal pressure

Upper and lower diverticula share a pressure-related mechanism; the middle one is the odd man out.

Mnemonic TNT — True = Traction (middle); Zenker (upper) and epiphrenic (lower) = false pulsion.

Notes

Zenker diverticulum

ANATOMY & MECHANISM
Herniation occurs through Killian's triangle / dehiscence — between the oblique fibers of thyropharyngeus and the transverse fibers of cricopharyngeus, an area anatomically lacking muscle.
A hypertonic upper esophageal sphincter raises distal pressure → mucosa and submucosa herniate through the weak point.
Usually degenerative → typically elderly patients, especially in their 70s–80s.

Clinical features

Sensation of food sticking in the throat.
Excessive salivation.
Intermittent dysphagia.
Cough.
Retained food/fluid in the pouch → aspiration.
Aspiration pneumonia — particularly dangerous in the elderly; may progress to lung abscess.

Diagnosis

TEST OF CHOICE
Barium esophagogram / swallow — it directly shows the diverticulum, which is the consequence of the underlying sphincter dysfunction. Manometry is generally not needed, and is difficult to position reliably at the upper esophagus.
ENDOSCOPY: NOT ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED
Often described as contraindicated, but the professor emphasized it is not absolutely so.
Safety rule: never push against resistance or advance blindly.
Benefits: evaluate the lower esophagus, look for reflux disease/Barrett, and exclude malignancy — longstanding food stasis raises squamous cell carcinoma risk.

Treatment

THE ESSENTIAL PRINCIPLE
Cricopharyngeal (upper esophageal) myotomy is the most important step — without it, expect recurrence or a postoperative leak and sepsis.
The diverticulum itself may then be resected (diverticulectomy).
For a pouch ≤ 2 cm, diverticulectomy may be unnecessary — myotomy alone can let the pouch empty and reintegrate functionally.
The procedure may be surgical or endoscopic.
